title: Subsets
problemStatement: Given an integer array nums of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set). The solution set must not contain duplicate subsets.
approachSteps: Every element has exactly two states: included in a given subset, or not — that binary choice per element is the core of the backtracking exploration.
Build subsets incrementally: at each step, you're deciding whether to include the next number in the array.

Use backtracking: at each index, first record the current partial subset as a valid answer (every partial state is itself a full, valid subset), then try including nums[index], recurse into the rest, then 'un-include' it (backtrack) and move to the next index without it.
Because you record the subset BEFORE deciding on the current element, you naturally capture subsets of every size, including the empty set at the very start.

bruteForce.approach: Iteratively double the result list: for each new number, add it to a copy of every existing subset (bit-manipulation / iterative doubling is also a valid non-backtracking approach here).

optimalApproach: Backtracking: recursively decide include/exclude for each element, recording every partial subset along the way. (Time is inherently O(n * 2^n) since that's the size of the output itself.)
solutionCode:
def subsets(nums):
    result = []
    path = []

    def backtrack(index):
        result.append(path.copy())  # record the current subset
        for i in range(index, len(nums)):
            path.append(nums[i])
            backtrack(i + 1)
            path.pop()  # undo the choice (backtrack)

    backtrack(0)
    return result
timeComplexity: O(n * 2^n) — there are 2^n subsets total, and copying each into the result costs O(n).
spaceComplexity: O(n * 2^n) for the output (unavoidable — that's the answer's size); O(n) additional for the recursion stack/path.
followUps: How would you handle duplicate numbers in the input while avoiding duplicate subsets in the output (Subsets II)?
How would you generate subsets iteratively using bitmasks from 0 to 2^n - 1 instead of recursive backtracking?

title: Permutations
problemStatement: Given an array nums of distinct integers, return all possible permutations. You can return the answer in any order.
approachSteps: Unlike subsets (include/exclude), a permutation needs EVERY element placed exactly once, in some order — the choice at each step is 'which unused element goes next.'
Track which numbers have already been used in the current partial permutation (a 'used' set or boolean array, or remove-and-restore from a working list).
Backtrack: at each position in the permutation being built, try every not-yet-used number, place it, recurse to fill the remaining positions, then remove it (backtrack) and try the next candidate.
When the partial permutation reaches the full length of nums, it's a complete, valid permutation — record a copy of it.

bruteForce.approach: There isn't a meaningfully simpler brute force — backtracking IS the standard approach; the only real 'brute force' variant is generating with library permutation functions rather than by hand.

optimalApproach: Backtracking that tracks used elements, builds one permutation position at a time, and records complete permutations once the working path reaches full length.
solutionCode:
def permute(nums):
    result = []
    path = []
    used = [False] * len(nums)

    def backtrack():
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            result.append(path.copy())
            return
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            used[i] = True
            path.append(nums[i])
            backtrack()
            path.pop()
            used[i] = False

    backtrack()
    return result
timeComplexity: O(n * n!) — there are n! permutations, each taking O(n) to copy into the result.
spaceComplexity: O(n * n!) for the output; O(n) additional for the used array and recursion depth.
followUps: How would you handle duplicate numbers in the input while avoiding duplicate permutations in the output (Permutations II)?
How would you generate the k-th permutation directly, without generating all of them?

title: N-Queens
problemStatement: The n-queens puzzle is placing n queens on an n x n chessboard such that no two queens attack each other (no shared row, column, or diagonal). Return all distinct solutions, each represented as a list of strings showing the board.
approachSteps: Since no two queens can share a row, you can simplify the problem: place exactly one queen per row, and decide which COLUMN it goes in for each row in turn.
That reframes an n^2-cell placement problem into an n-step decision problem (one column choice per row), which is what makes backtracking tractable.
Track which columns, and which 'diagonals' (there are two families: row - col constant, and row + col constant) are already occupied, so you can check a candidate placement in O(1).
For each row, try every column: if that column and both diagonals through this cell are free, place the queen, mark them occupied, and recurse to the next row.
If recursing from that placement leads to a dead end, backtrack: remove the queen, unmark the column/diagonals, and try the next column in this row.
When all n rows have a queen placed validly, record the current board configuration as one solution.

bruteForce.approach: Try every possible placement of n queens on n^2 cells without the row-per-queen simplification, checking all pairs for attacks.
bruteForce.timeComplexity: O(n^(2n)) or worse — combinatorially far larger

optimalApproach: Backtracking with one queen per row, using O(1) column/diagonal occupancy checks (via sets) to prune invalid branches as early as possible.
solutionCode:
def solve_n_queens(n):
    results = []
    cols = set()
    diag1 = set()  # row - col
    diag2 = set()  # row + col
    board = [['.'] * n for _ in range(n)]

    def backtrack(row):
        if row == n:
            results.append([''.join(r) for r in board])
            return
        for col in range(n):
            if col in cols or (row - col) in diag1 or (row + col) in diag2:
                continue
            cols.add(col)
            diag1.add(row - col)
            diag2.add(row + col)
            board[row][col] = 'Q'

            backtrack(row + 1)

            cols.remove(col)
            diag1.remove(row - col)
            diag2.remove(row + col)
            board[row][col] = '.'

    backtrack(0)
    return results
timeComplexity: O(n!) in the worst case (roughly — the branching factor shrinks by row due to pruning, bounded by n! total placements); each valid solution recorded costs O(n^2) to serialize.
spaceComplexity: O(n^2) for the board, plus O(n) for the constraint sets and recursion depth.
followUps: Why are diagonals tracked as row - col and row + col specifically — what property of a diagonal does each capture?
How would you solve just 'count the number of solutions' (N-Queens II) more cheaply, without building/storing every board string?
